S.G.B. v. S.J.L.

[Indexed as: B. (S.G.) v. L. (S.J.)]

102 O.R. (3d) 197

2010 ONSC 3717

Ontario Superior Court of Justice,

Mesbur J.

June 30, 2010

Family law -- Custody -- Deliberate alienation -- Father deliberately alienating child from mother -- Mother granted sole custody of child with authority to obtain any treatment and/or intervention for him that she deeded necessary -- Father, father's friend, child's older brother and child's psychiatrist prohibited from contacting child for period of three months.
Family law -- Support -- Child support -- Mother receiving one-time taxable dividend and her personal investment company receiving one-time non-taxable dividend in 2006 -- Neither payment included in mother's 2006 income for purpose of
Federal Child Support Guidelines
income calculation.
The parties separated when L was eight and J was four. Both children initially lived primarily with their mother, but both eventually left her home and moved in with their father. They rejected the mother and refused to see her. The parties agreed to binding arbitration to resolve their parenting issues. The arbitrator found that the father had deliberately alienated the children against the mother and that the only remedy was to award sole custody of the children to the mother, with no access to the father. The father's appeal was allowed. The appeal judge upheld the finding of deliberate alienation, but found that the arbitrator had made errors of law in determining the appropriate remedy. When the appeal was heard, L was about to turn 18. The appeal judge found that she did not have an adequate evidentiary basis to determine what remedy would be in J's best interests and that the best course would be to have a trial judge hear the issue of disposition in light of the arbitrator's findings of fact. Issues  of custody and child support were before the trial judge.
Held, the mother should be awarded sole custody of J.
The evidence pointed overwhelmingly to a change in custody. In cases of severe irrational alienation such as this one, all the experts recommend that the child be removed from the care of the alienating parent. The mother had the ability, the strength and the insight to parent J appropriately. Unlike the father, she put J's interests before her own. The mother was specifically authorized to obtain any treatment and/or intervention for J as she, in her sole discretion, deemed necessary and appropriate for J's best interests. For a period of three months, the father, L, the father's friend and J's psychiatrist were prohibited from attempting to communicate with J, and J was prohibited from attempting to communicate with them.
The mother was the beneficiary of a family trust which in turn owned a personal investment corporation. In calculating the mother's income for the purposes of the
Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175
, a taxable dividend which she received in 2006 and a non-taxable dividend that the corporation received in 2006 were not included in income. The taxable dividend was a one-time payment and would not recur. The non-taxable dividend was also a one-time receipt, and those funds were the corporation's only asset and made up the mother's ongoing source of income. Based on the amounts payable by the mother under the Guidelines, the mother had overpaid child support after the children moved in with the father. She was not seeking to recover the amount of the overpayment. [page198]
RULING on custody and child support.

MESBUR J.:--
Introduction and Factual Background

[
1
] This case sadly raises again the difficult issue of how
to deal with a situation in which a child has been deliberately
alienated from a parent. Here, the father, SGB, severely
undermined and destroyed his sons' relationship with their
mother, SJL. The arbitrator who conducted an arbitration for
the parties concluded this is a case of irrational alienation
from a parent. The judge who heard the appeal from the
arbitration agreed. The fact of irrational alienation is not in
dispute. While the problem is obvious, the potential solution
is not.

[
2
] The father, now 61, and mother, 55, married in 1984 and
separated in 1998. They have two sons, LB, born in 1991, and
[page199] JB, born in 1994. At the time the parties
separated, LB was eight and JB was only four. LB turned 19 on
June 22, 2010 and JB's 16th birthday was June 11.

[
3
] The parties have been in litigation about the boys and
financial matters for more than a decade. They mediated their
contentious issue in 1998. This resulted in a parenting plan
that became part of a court order in 1999. Their divorce
followed shortly after. In 2003, they returned to mediation and
again agreed on a parenting plan. Both parenting plans had the
children living primarily with their mother and having frequent
and regular access with their father. Following the separation,
the mother and the children remained in the matrimonial home.

[
4
] Notwithstanding their agreement, the parties had ongoing
difficulties in co-parenting their children. In the autumn of
2004, LB left his mother's home and moved in with his father.
LB was 13 at the time. In his evidence at this trial, father
explained that LB reported his reason for leaving his mother's
home was he was tired of constantly arguing with her, it
overwhelmed him and he couldn't cope with it. Father took no
steps to return LB to his primary residence with his mother.

[
5
] After LB moved, JB began to act out at his mother's home,
particularly around transitions from his father's home to his
mother's. Jewish Family and Child Services ("JFCS") became
involved with the family. They eventually suggested to the
mother that she might consider hiring trained child-care
workers to assist her with JB's behaviour. She did so. Father,
whose background involved working for the Children's Aid
Society with disturbed children in a residential setting, did
not support mother's efforts to manage JB in her home with the
assistance of the workers; to the contrary, he undermined her
and them.

[
6
] Matters escalated. In January of 2006, JB ran away from
his mother's house to his father's. He was only 11. He repeated
this on two occasions shortly after. On the last occasion,
father did not return him, or require him to return to his
mother's. JB has remained in his father's home since the
beginning of March of 2006. This marked the beginning of both
boys' increasing resistance to spend time with their mother,
culminating in a virtual refusal to do so.

[
7
] The parties engaged mediators, parent coordinators,
lawyers and various mental health professionals in their quest
to resolve their difficulties. Even though many mental health
professionals have intervened, the boys have utterly rejected
their mother. They actively refuse to see her, call her "mom",
thank her for gifts, or answer her letters or cards. Mother,
however, continues to pay child support for them, and has paid
for all [page200] their extracurricular activities, as well as
private school, therapy and all their uninsured medical and
dental costs. The children say she does not really love them.
They see her as simply trying to "buy" their affection by
supporting them.

[
8
] Mother continues to try to have a relationship with the
children. She writes letters, cards for birthdays and holidays,
and sends brief text messages from time to time. The children
rarely respond. She attends all the children's parent-teacher
meetings, school concerts and events and both boys'
graduations. The children ignore her.

[
9
] After failing at a third attempt to mediate their
parenting issues, the parties finally submitted these issues to
arbitration. They participated in binding arbitration before
Dr. Ted Horowitz in 2008. In the arbitration, the mother sought
an order awarding her sole custody of the children, together
with the authority to make all treatment decisions for them. As
one of the treatments, the mother wanted to require the
children to participate in a therapeutic intervention called
"Family Bridges: A Workshop for Troubled and Alienated
Parent-Child Relationships". Counsel and the parties referred
to this programme as the "Workshop". In their submission to
arbitration, the parents specifically empowered the arbitrator
to consider the issue of whether the children should
participate in the Workshop.

[
10
] After a six-day oral hearing, Dr. Horowitz found the
father had deliberately alienated the children against their
mother. The arbitrator set out in great detail the history of
this case and the facts supporting his finding. I will not
repeat them here. After reviewing all his factual findings, the
arbitrator held there "is more than sufficient evidence to
conclude that [mother] as the 'target parent' is the
intentional victim of irrational alienation by her sons, [LB]
and [JB], designed and orchestrated by [father]". Dr. Horowitz
concluded "[father] has an understanding of what has transpired
and is fully aware of his role . . . he feels no guilt, remorse
or regret over the situation he has created". [See Note 1 below]

[
11
] The arbitrator determined that the only remedy was to
award sole custody of the children to their mother, with no
access by their father and those other individuals who were
deemed to have participated with father (whether deliberately
or unwittingly) in the father's campaign of alienation. The
arbitration award also permitted the mother to have the
children participate in the Workshop. [page201]

[
12
] The father appealed the arbitrator's decision and also
sought judicial review of it. Herman J., who heard both the
appeal and judicial review, dismissed the application for
judicial review, but allowed the appeal on a question of law
[
2009 CanLII 4523 (ON SC)
, [2009] O.J. No. 515, 66 R.F.L. (6th) 81 (S.C.J.)]. After
reviewing the arbitration award in detail, Herman J. concluded
that the arbitrator had erred in law in two ways:
(a) when he decided not to order a new custody assessment, the
arbitrator wrongly considered two factors: first, the
arbitrator considered an assessment report from the late
Dr. Awad that he had ruled inadmissible in the arbitration,
and second, the arbitrator considered his own personal
experience as an assessor; and
(b) he did not sufficiently consider the particular
circumstances of the case, namely, the extremity of the
remedy of a change in custody coupled with participation in
the Workshop, JB's special needs and the potential impact
on him of separation from his older brother.

[
13
] Justice Herman then heard the parties' submissions as to
the appropriate disposition in light of these findings. In
reasons delivered May 14, 2009 [
2009 CanLII 24230 (ON SC)
, [2009] O.J. No. 1998, 66 R.F.L.
(6th) 103 (S.C.J.)], she held [at para. 47]:

The legal errors in the arbitration award concerned the
remedy for parental alienation, not the finding that parental
alienation had occurred. In reaching my decision on
disposition, I have considered the desirability of addressing
the estrangement between the mother and her children.
However, the problem with fashioning an appropriate remedy is
that I do not have an adequate evidentiary basis to enable me
to determine what remedy would be in J.B.'s best interests.

[
14
] Finally, Justice Herman concluded that she had to set
aside the entire award, and decided the best course would be to
have a trial judge hear the issue of disposition in light of
the arbitrator's findings of fact. She held that if either
party wished to proceed to a trial, the trial should be
expedited.

[
15
] Both parties sought leave to appeal Herman J.'s
decision. Both were denied leave. Some time later, the parties
finally agreed to have Dr. Sol Goldstein conduct an up to date
custody and access assessment. They also agreed to a trial, if
necessary. Dr. Goldstein completed the assessment and delivered
his report on April 15, 2010. Mother agreed with Dr.
Goldstein's recommendations, which echoed, in large part, the
arbitrator's. Father did not. Since they could not reach an
agreement concerning the children, a trial was necessary. This
is that trial. [page202]
The Issues for This Trial and the Parties' Positions on Them

[
16
] There are two broad issues in this trial, custody of JB
and child support for both children. In order to streamline the
trial before me, the parties agreed that all of the evidence
taken before the arbitrator, as well as Dr. Barbara Jo Fidler's
evidence before Justice Herman, would form part of the
evidentiary record before me. They agreed the oral evidence at
this trial would focus on updating the court on events since
the arbitration.

[
17
] Since the arbitration award and Justice Herman's
decision both set out the background facts of this case in
great detail, I will not repeat them here, unless some of those
factual findings are necessary to explain my analysis and my
decision.

The custody issue -- overview

[
18
] Since this began as a divorce action, the issues of
custody, access and child support are governed by the provisions
of the
Divorce Act
[See Note 2 below] and the
Federal Child
Support Guidelines
. [See Note 3 below]

[
19
]
Section 16
of the
Divorce Act
deals with the court's
ability to make an order concerning custody of or the access to
any children of the marriage. Subsections (8), (9) and (10)
have bearing on the issues in this case. They read:

Factors

16(8) In making an order under this section, the court
shall take into consideration only the best interests of the
child of the marriage as determined by reference to the
condition, means, needs and other circumstances of the child.

Past conduct

16(9) In making an order under this section, the court
shall not take into consideration the past conduct of any
person unless the conduct is relevant to the ability of that
person to act as a parent of a child.

Maximum contact

16(10) In making an order under this section, the court
shall give effect to the principle that a child of the
marriage should have as much contact with each spouse as is
consistent with the best interests of the child and, for that
purpose, shall take into consideration the willingness of the
person for whom custody is sought to facilitate such contact.

[
20
] Therefore, determining the appropriate custody order
involves deciding what is in JB's best interests, in the
context of the finding that his father has deliberately
alienated him from [page203] his mother. Since LB is now over
the age of majority, I cannot make a custody or access award in
relation to him.

[
21
] In light of Herman J.'s findings on the appeal, I must
consider, along with all other necessary factors, JB's special
needs and the potential impact on him of a separation from his
brother if I find changing custody to his mother would be in
his best interests. Considering JB's best interests must also
address whether they would be met by his participating in the
Workshop.

[
22
] In mother's view, the assessor's recommendations meet
JB's best interests. This would involve transferring custody of
JB to her, permitting her to have JB participate in the
Workshop and cutting off all JB's access to his father and
brother, as well as his therapist Dr. Harman and his father's
friend Nila, until JB has completed the programme, and the
court decides it is in his interests to resume contact with
them, and under what conditions.

[
23
] To the contrary, father is content with the current
arrangement for JB, and for that matter, for LB as well. He
sees the children remaining with him. He suggests that the
mother should have input on all educational and medical
decisions concerning the children, and she should continue to
make all the necessary medical and dental appointments for
them. In addition, father says that mother should seek
counselling and that JB could participate in the process.
Father also seems to suggest he and LB might participate in
counselling as well, but that is not entirely clear.

[
24
] Father, however, is vehemently opposed to the Workshop,
and JB's participation in it. If I order JB to participate, the
father will not attend himself, even though experts in the
Workshop say it works best and is most successful when both
parents take part. Father says it would even be fruitless to
insist that JB participate, either.

[
25
] This brings me to the question of whether one can insist
JB participate, or "force" him to attend the Workshop. Since JB
has just turned 16, he presents certain challenges. [See Note 4
below] A 16-year old, in some circumstances, is considered a
"mature minor", capable of some autonomous decision-making. JB
has the notion he cannot be "forced" to see his mother, or
participate in a process that might assist him in
re-establishing a meaningful relationship with her. Regardless
of JB's age, however, the court still has jurisdiction over him.
He is a child with special needs, remains in full-time
attendance at school and is under the age of majority. By
definition, [See Note 5 below] he is a "child of the marriage",
about [page204] whom the court may make an order for custody. I
will have more to say about "coercion" later in these reasons
when I address some of the particular issues surrounding the
Workshop.

[
26
] In short, I expect JB to comply with any order I make.
Court orders must be followed. JB is not the one to decide what
is in his best interests. His parents have failed in their
responsibility to do so; that task falls to me instead, and I
will therefore decide what is best for him.

The child support issue -- overview

[
27
] The second issue involves deciding the appropriate
disposition of child support, both retroactive and prospective,
in relation to both children. As far as child support is
concerned,
s. 15.1
of the
Divorce Act
permits the court to make
an order requiring a spouse to pay for the support of any or
all of the children of the marriage. Subsection (3) requires
the court to do so in accordance with the applicable
guidelines. In this case, that means the
Federal Child Support
Guidelines
.

[
28
] Mother takes the position she has overpaid her past
obligations, while father takes the position that she has
underpaid. Prospective child support, of course, will depend on
two things: first, the custodial arrangement for JB; and
second, the appropriate child support for LB, who is now over
the age of majority.
Parental Alienation and the Workshop as a Remedy for It

What is parental alienation?

[
29
] The concept of "parental alienation" and using the
Workshop to treat it inform all of this litigation. Mother sees
the Workshop as the only hope for repairing her relationship
with her sons. Father sees it as untested "junk science" that
will irrevocably damage JB.

[
30
] There is, and has been, much controversy about whether a
condition called Parental Alienation Syndrome ("PAS") exists as
a discreet psychiatric "syndrome". The American Psychiatric
Association has not yet included PAS as an accepted syndrome in
the DSM. That said, all the child psychiatrists who testified
confirmed that they see clinical situations in which a parent
has been alienated from a child, either for what is obviously a
good reason, or, more rarely, for no objectively good reason.

[
31
] Cases with no objectively good reason for alienation, or
cases where a child's reaction in completely rejecting a parent
is totally out of proportion to that parent's conduct are
called "irrational" parental alienation. The arbitrator held
that this is one of those cases of irrational parental
alienation. Whether this [page205] case is one of Parental
Alienation Syndrome or simply a case of irrational parental
alienation is of no moment.

[
32
] Repairing JB's relationship with his mother is clearly
in his best interests. His own treating psychiatrist testified
that "of course" it is in his best interests to have a
relationship with his mother. The question is how to accomplish
this. Mother says changing custody to her and having JB
participate in the Workshop or something like it is the only
way to do so.

What does the Workshop entail, and what other modalities are
available?

[
33
] Dr. Richard Warshak is a clinical research and
consultant psychologist. He received his Ph.D. in clinical
psychology in 1978. He has many years of experience in clinical
psychology, including as staff psychologist for the Dallas
Child Guidance Clinic. He is also a clinical full professor of
psychology at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical
Center in the Department of Psychiatry. Dr. Warshak has written
extensively about irrational parental alienation and has had
many articles published in peer-reviewed journals. The Workshop
began in around 1991, and Dr. Warshak has been a part of the
project since 2005. He has participated in many workshops with
many alienated children and their "target" parent.

[
34
] Dr. Warshak testified at the arbitration about the
Workshop and parental alienation in general. He was qualified
as an expert to provide opinion evidence about these issues. He
could not offer an opinion about the B children in particular,
since he had not met them, or their father.

[
35
] Dr. Warshak described the Workshop as designed to
accelerate alienated children's adjustment to being with the
alienated parent, with the goal of helping them repair and
maintain a healthy relationship with both parents. He said a
primary goal is to give children a face-saving way to rapidly
restore a positive relationship with the parents. The programme
also involves a parenting component for participating parents,
so they can develop and improve necessary nurturing and
communication skills.

[
36
] A fundamental part of the Workshop is to separate the
child from the alienating parent. Dr. Warshak said it is
important to provide some measure of restriction of contact
between the children and the favoured parent until the children
have the ability to repair and maintain a healthy relationship
with the parent they had been rejecting.

[
37
] The programme runs an average of about four days, with
frequent breaks, and the use of varied materials. Dr. Warshak
testified the children are treated with respect and dignity,
and [page206] are not held against their will. The Workshop
often takes place in a relaxed, recreational setting.
Importantly, Dr. Warshak said the programme works best when
both parents choose to participate in it.

[
38
] Although Dr. Warshak has not met either the father or
the children, he has met with the mother and provided advice to
her since around 2004. He has educated her about both parental
alienation and the Workshop. Father complains that as a result,
mother has become somewhat obsessive about PAS in general, and
the Workshop in particular. He describes everything she does as
on "the PAS model". He says all her actions are guided by those
who subscribe to the theory, and this colours all her actions.
He says if only she would consider a non-PAS-aligned therapist,
this would take the situation "light years" ahead.

[
39
] To some extent, the father is right. There is no
question that mother believes her children have been
deliberately alienated against her. The arbitrator found this
as a fact, and I agree. Mother has therefore enlisted the help
of mental health professionals who have some expertise in
dealing with families in which this tragic situation exists.
That she has picked up their theories and jargon is not
surprising. That she follows their advice quite scrupulously is
also not surprising. While some might view her actions as
overly rigid, and would simply say give the children what they
want, see them under their terms if and when that happens, this
is contrary to the advice she receives from the experts. Since
mother has been searching for years to find tools to assist her
in reunifying with her boys, I do not fault her for trying the
methods the experts suggest to her. This has included following
Dr. Warshak's advice about how an alienated parent should deal
with his or her alienated children.

[
40
] Dr. Barbara Jo Fidler, who testified before Herman J. to
assist her in determining the appropriate disposition of the
appeal, has also had experience with the Workshop. Dr. Sol
Goldstein, who performed the custody assessment for this trial,
and testified at it, also has experience with children who have
participated in the Workshop.

[
41
] Dr. Fidler has written extensively on how to deal with
challenging issues in child custody disputes, and particularly
about alienated children in parental separations. She
recognized that the order mother seeks has an element of
coercion in it. She addressed this issue in the particular
context of adolescents, such as JB. She testified:

. . . children are coerced in society to do many things by
their parents, by the law. There's lots of things . . .
adolescents can't do . . . We need to allow children the
ability to save face and for them to say, well, the judge made
me do [page207] it, frankly, and let them go into this process
. . . so in adolescents in particular, this whole issue of,
you know, children's wishes, and when they're adolescents they
should decide, and as I have said, adolescents aren't allowed
to decide many things, and adolescents' brains, as we
understand them, are under construction. That's why we see
more risk-taking behaviour in adolescents. That's why we see
impulse control problems. That's why we see judgment problems
with adolescents . . . Adolescents don't necessarily make the
best decisions. So it strikes me as particularly interesting
that somehow they're afforded and by some feel that they
should be making these big, huge decisions about severing ties
with a parent. [See Note 6 below]

[
42
] Dr. Fidler also addressed the issue of the effectiveness
of counselling in cases of irrational alienation. She said
"therapy and counselling with an alienated child does not
work in severe cases when the child is continuing to have
contact with the alienating or favoured parent. There needs to
be an interruption in that contact. The goal is ultimately to
resume that contact so the child can have a relationship with
both parents." [See Note 7 below]

[
43
] She went on to say, "We know from our failures, so many
failures, it is just almost unbelievable to see how quickly an
alienated child before your eyes can, once they're out of the
orbit of the favoured parent, can begin to relate positively to
the rejected parent and to give and receive love." [See Note 8
below]

[
44
] Sadly, the reverse is also true. As Dr. Fidler put it,
"And it's just as unbelievable to see, unless it was before
your own eyes, that child is anticipating contact with the
favoured parent. So they [the favoured parent] come to the
therapy to pick the child up, or it's just before the
transition in terms of parenting time, switch back to being
alienated before your eyes." [See Note 9 below]

[
45
] It is for this reason Dr. Fidler opined, "There needs to
be a period of stabilization and reintegration with the
rejected parent without the child going back into the orbit of
the favoured parent for a period of time, and then we
reintegrate back the favoured parent, hopefully. That's the
ultimate goal." [See Note 10 below]

[
46
] Dr. Sol Goldstein conducted a custody assessment for the
parties after the decision on the appeal. The parties retained
Dr. Goldstein jointly. Dr. Goldstein has been a member of the
department of psychiatry at the University of Toronto, Faculty
of [page208] Medicine since 1968. He currently holds the rank
of assistant professor. He has practised as a child
psychiatrist for more than 40 years, and has a wealth of
experience with divorcing and separating families, and with
custody and access assessments. He was qualified as an expert
at this trial to provide the court with his expert opinion
concerning JB's best interests.

[
47
] Dr. Goldstein shares the view that irrationally
alienated children must be separated from the alienating parent
for a period of time in order to repair the relationship with
the other parent. He, too, commented on the almost instant
transformation of some children once they are removed from the
alienating parent's care.
